--- title: "Inventory" --- Housing stock, occupancy and vacancy, structure type, year built, and building permits for the Richmond region. Stock figures come from the ACS 5-year estimates; production figures from the Census Building Permits Survey. ::: callout-note ## Two different things **Stock** is what exists — the ACS count of housing units standing in a five-year window. **Production** is what was permitted — an administrative count of permits *issued*, which leads completions by a year or more and can be cancelled. The two never reconcile exactly, and neither is a count of units built. Read them as separate series. ::: ## The region added housing, but the expansion ring grew faster than the core ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](inventory_files/figure-html/fig-units-trend-1.png){#fig-units-trend fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of total housing units in the three core Richmond localities and the pooled expansion ring across three ACS windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024. Every geography grows across the period; Chesterfield adds the most units while the four-locality expansion ring grows fastest in percentage terms.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The three core localities held 404,918 housing units in the 2024 window, up 13.3% from the 2014 window. - The four-locality expansion ring grew 18.4% over the same decade — faster in percentage terms than the core, from a much smaller base. - Chesterfield added the most units of any single locality, growing 17.1% while Henrico grew 8.3%. - Richmond city grew 15.3%, second-fastest among the core three despite being the most built-out. ::: {#tbl-units .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Sussex County and Petersburg city have the highest rates, near 20 and 16 percent; Chesterfield and Hanover have the lowest, under 5 percent.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Sussex County (19.6%) and Petersburg city (16.2%) have the region's highest vacancy rates — both are southern localities with declining or flat housing demand. - Chesterfield's 3.8% is the region's lowest, and Hanover (4.3%) is close behind; the suburban core runs tight. - Richmond city sits at 8.7%, above the pooled core's 5.7% but slightly below Virginia's 8.7%. - The pooled expansion ring (5.2%) and core (5.7%) are nearly identical, so the spread in this chart is driven almost entirely by the outer southern localities. ::: {#tbl-vacancy-reason .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Vacant units by reason, 2024 ACS 5-year. Cells with a coefficient of variation above 30 are suppressed (—); * marks a medium-reliability estimate (CV 15-30). Source: ACS Table B25004.
Reason vacant Chesterfield Henrico Richmond city Richmond core
For rent 1,830 2,924 3,911 8,665
For sale only 661* 500* 436* 1,597
For seasonal, recreational, or occasional use — 274* 457* 821*
Other vacant 2,183 2,610 2,971 7,764
Rented, not occupied — 546* 992 1,926
Sold, not occupied 402* 697* 1,205* 2,304
````` ::: ::: - "For rent" is the largest vacancy category in every core locality — 39.2% of Richmond city's vacant units and 38.7% of Henrico's. - "Other vacant" is the second-largest everywhere, at 29.8% to 39.3% of vacant units; it is the Census catch-all for units that are neither on the market nor seasonal, and it includes long-term-abandoned stock. - Units held off market ("other vacant" plus seasonal) account for roughly a third of core vacancy, so the effective *available* vacancy rate is well below the headline number. - Chesterfield's for-sale vacancies (661) outnumber Henrico's (500) despite Chesterfield's lower overall vacancy rate. ## The core is a single-family region; density is concentrated in the city ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](inventory_files/figure-html/fig-structure-1.png){#fig-structure fig-align='left' fig-alt='Stacked horizontal bar chart of housing units by structure type for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the pooled core, and the pooled expansion ring in 2024. Single-family detached dominates everywhere, at 88 percent in the expansion ring and 78 percent in Chesterfield, but only 45 percent in Richmond city, where buildings with 20 or more units make up 22 percent of the stock.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Single-family detached homes are 63.0% of the pooled core's stock and 87.8% of the expansion ring's. - Richmond city is the outlier: 21.6% of its units sit in buildings of 20 or more, against 7.2% in Henrico and 4.6% in Chesterfield. - Small multifamily (2–4 units) is scarce everywhere but the city, where it is 12.0% of stock versus 2.9% in Chesterfield and 0.9% in the expansion ring. - Manufactured housing is a rounding error in the core (0.7%) but 2.5% of the expansion ring and 12.6% of Ashland's stock. ::: callout-warning ## Small-geography reliability Ashland is a town of roughly 3,164 housing units, so its ACS estimates carry wide margins of error — 2 of its 11 structure-type and year-built cells fall below the CV-30 reliability threshold. Ashland and the four expansion-ring localities are shown here only where the underlying estimate is reliable; suppressed cells appear as an em dash. ::: ## Housing age splits the region in two ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](inventory_files/figure-html/fig-year-built-1.png){#fig-year-built fig-align='left' fig-alt='Stacked horizontal bar chart of housing units by construction era for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the pooled core, and the pooled expansion ring in 2024. Richmond city\'s stock is oldest, with 38 percent built before 1950; Chesterfield and the expansion ring are newest, with over half built since 1990.' width=100%} ::: ::: - 37.7% of Richmond city's housing was built before 1950, against 7.4% in Henrico and 2.4% in Chesterfield. - Chesterfield's stock is the region's newest: 50.3% was built in 1990 or later, and 17.2% since 2010. - The expansion ring is newer still by that measure — 56.0% built since 1990 — consistent with its faster unit growth. - Only 13.2% of the pooled core's stock dates from 2010 or later, so the great majority of the region's housing predates the current market. ## Permitting recovered from the 2011 trough, and what gets permitted has changed ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](inventory_files/figure-html/fig-permits-trend-1.png){#fig-permits-trend fig-align='left' fig-alt='Stacked area chart of annually permitted housing units in the 17-locality Richmond region from 2000 to 2025, split into single-family and multifamily. Single-family dominates the early 2000s, both collapse after 2007 to a 2011 trough of 2,520 units, and the recovery is driven by multifamily, which exceeds single-family for the first time in 2022.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Regional permitting peaked at 10,414 units in 2022 and bottomed at 2,520 in 2011 — a 76% collapse. - The 2025 total of 9,091 units is still below the 2022 peak, but roughly 3.6 times the trough. - Multifamily was 3.6% of permitted units in 2000 and 51.6% in 2025; it first exceeded single-family in 2022. - Single-family permitting has been flat at roughly 4,400–5,900 units a year since 2020, so essentially all of the swing in regional volume is multifamily. ::: {#tbl-permits-5yr .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Expansion ring (4 localities) 6,719 371 7,090 5.2%
Hanover County 2,466 326 2,792 11.7%
New Kent County 1,865 35 1,900 1.8%
Goochland County 1,582 0 1,582 0.0%
Powhatan County 806 10 816 1.2%
King William County 802 9 811 1.1%
Prince George County 521 16 537 3.0%
Petersburg (Independent City) 217 271 488 55.5%
Dinwiddie County 351 0 351 0.0%
Amelia County 291 2 293 0.7%
Sussex County 171 0 171 0.0%
King and Queen County 168 0 168 0.0%

````` ::: ::: - Over the last five years the core three localities accounted for 37,448 of the region's 47,667 permitted units — 79% of regional production. - Richmond city permitted 9,126 multifamily units in five years, more than Henrico (7,549) and Chesterfield (5,857), despite being the smallest of the three by stock. - Chesterfield is the region's single-family engine, with 8,902 single-family permits — more than double Henrico's. - The expansion ring permitted 6,719 single-family units against only 371 multifamily, a 5.2% multifamily share. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](inventory_files/figure-html/fig-permits-core-1.png){#fig-permits-core fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of the multifamily share of permitted units for Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield from 2015 to 2025. Richmond city rises from about 51 percent to 86 percent, Henrico is volatile between 25 and 73 percent, and Chesterfield falls back to under 30 percent after a 2022 peak.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Richmond city's multifamily share rose from 50.7% in 2015 to 86.3% in 2025 — the city now permits almost nothing but apartments. - Chesterfield peaked at 57.2% multifamily in 2022 and fell back to 28.2% by 2025, returning to a single-family pattern. - Henrico is the most volatile of the three, swinging between 24.5% (2016) and 73.4% (2023). - The three localities diverged after 2021: before then their multifamily shares moved roughly together, and since then they have not. ::: callout-tip ## What this page establishes The Richmond region's existing stock is overwhelmingly single-family and largely predates 1990, with density and prewar housing both concentrated in Richmond city. New production tells a different story — since 2022 the region has permitted more multifamily than single-family units, driven almost entirely by the city and Henrico, while the expansion ring continues to build detached houses almost exclusively. Vacancy is low across the core and the ring, so the stock that exists is being used; the region's slack sits in its southern localities. The [Demographics](demographics.qmd) and [Market](market.qmd) pages cover who lives in this housing and what it costs. :::
